claims.text: Increasing atomic size mismatch in equimolar high-entropy nanoalloys promotes local chemical ordering during high-temperature exposure.
Local chemical ordering caused by atomic size mismatch accelerates phase segregation.
Phase segregation destabilizes the disordered solid solution.
Keeping the alloys equimolar keeps their configurational entropy constant.
Larger atomic size differences create local strain and lattice distortion.
Local strain and lattice distortion enhance local chemical ordering.
At high temperature, local chemical inhomogeneities drive segregation or the formation of intermetallic regions.
Large configurational entropy does not necessarily prevent structural and chemical instability caused by the proposed mismatch-mediated process.
High-mismatch alloys will show an earlier onset of local chemical ordering than the low-mismatch baseline.
High-mismatch alloys will develop more extensive local chemical ordering than the low-mismatch baseline.
High-mismatch alloys will show an earlier onset of phase segregation than the low-mismatch baseline.
High-mismatch alloys will develop more extensive phase segregation than the low-mismatch baseline.
The predicted mismatch-dependent destabilization applies only where atomic diffusion is significant.
At lower temperatures, or when impurities or external stresses vary, other stabilization mechanisms may dominate.
A statistically significant absence of earlier or more pronounced ordering and segregation in the high-mismatch series would falsify atomic size mismatch as the dominant mediator.

contradictions.description: The intervention calls the two series compositionally identical while varying atomic size mismatch, whereas the experimental design proposes selecting different elements to obtain low and high mismatch. Changing elemental identities changes composition; if the compositions are truly identical, atomic size mismatch cannot ordinarily be varied independently.
